**Supported Fact**

- Parsing lowercases the scheme: in `scheme start state` and `scheme state`, ASCII letters are appended to the buffer lowercased. For an HTTPS URL, that means `HTTPS:` becomes `https:`. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- `https` is a special scheme whose default port is `443`. In `port state`, if the parsed port equals the scheme’s default port, the URL record’s `port` is set to `null`; in serialization, a port is emitted only if it is non-null. So `:443` is normalized away in the parsed URL record and disappears on serialization. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- A non-opaque host is parsed by percent-decoding the host, UTF-8 decoding that result, and then running the domain parser. The domain parser uses Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing, and the standard gives examples such as `☕.example` becoming `xn--53h.example`; its host round-trip table also shows `faß.example` becoming `xn--fa-hia.example`. This means a Unicode hostname in an HTTPS URL is normalized to an ASCII IDNA form, not kept as raw Unicode in the serialized URL. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/, https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr46/tr46-35.html)
- For ASCII domains, the domain parser lowercases them, and the host round-trip table shows `EXAMPLE.COM` becoming `example.com`. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- Dot segments are normalized during path parsing. A single-dot path segment is `.` or an ASCII-case-insensitive match for `%2e`. A double-dot path segment is `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, or `%2e%2e` with ASCII-case-insensitive matching. In `path state`, a double-dot segment triggers “shorten url’s path”, which removes the last path segment; the spec’s note says `/usr/..` becomes `/`. Single-dot segments are omitted from the path, except that the algorithm may append an empty segment when needed at the end. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- The parser starts fragment parsing when it sees `#`. In `fragment state`, each fragment code point is UTF-8 percent-encoded with the fragment percent-enco

- Parsing lowercases the scheme: in `scheme start state` and `scheme state`, ASCII letters are appended to the buffer lowercased. For an HTTPS URL, that means `HTTPS:` becomes `https:`. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

So `:443` is normalized away in the parsed URL record and disappears on serialization. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- A non-opaque host is parsed by percent-decoding the host, UTF-8 decoding that result, and then running the domain parser. The domain parser uses Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing, and the standard gives examples such as `☕.example` becoming `xn--53h.example`; its host round-trip table also shows `faß.example` becoming `xn--fa-hia.example`. This means a Unicode hostname in an HTTPS URL is normalized to an ASCII IDNA form, not kept as raw Unicode in the serialized URL. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/, https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr46/tr46-35.html)
- For ASCII domains, the domain parser lowercases them, and the host round-trip table shows `EXAMPLE.COM` becoming `example.com`. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- Dot segments are normalized during path parsing. A single-dot path segment is `.` or an ASCII-case-insensitive match for `%2e`. A double-dot path segment is `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, or `%2e%2e` with ASCII-case-insensitive matching. In `path state`, a double-dot segment triggers “shorten url’s path”, which removes the last path segment; the spec’s note says `/usr/..` becomes `/`. Single-dot segments are omitted from the path, except that the algorithm may append an empty segment when needed at the end. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- The parser starts fragment parsing when it sees `#`. In `fragment state`, each fragment code point is UTF-8 percent-encoded with the fragment percent-encode set. That set includes the C0 control percent-encode set plus space, `"`, `<`, `>`, and `` ` ``; the C0 control percent-encode set includes all code points above `U+007E`, so non-ASCII fragment characters are percent-encoded too. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- In `path state`, non-separator path code points are UTF-8 percent-encoded with the path percent-encode set. The spec’s parsed-components table shows `file:///ada/Analytical%20Engine/README.md` producing a path segment `Analytical%20Engine`, which is direct evidence that `%20` remains percent-encoded in the stored path segment rather than being decoded to a space. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

**Inference**

- For already-valid percent-encoded path bytes such as `%66`, the current algorithm appears to preserve them rather than decode them to literal characters. Reason: `%` followed by two ASCII hex digits is accepted as a valid percent-encoded byte; the path parser then calls UTF-8 percent-encode with the path percent-encode set; that set does not include `%`; and the generic percent-encoding algorithm says characters not in the set are appended unchanged. On that reading, `%66` stays `%66`, not `f`. (Inference from https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- The same reasoning suggests there is no parsing-time normalization that uppercases the hex digits of an already-present path escape. For example, `%2f` appears to stay `%2f`, except that `%2e` and related spellings are specially recognized for dot-segment handling because the single-dot and double-dot definitions are ASCII-case-insensitive. (Inference from https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
- The same preservation inference also applies to valid percent-encoded bytes already present in the fragment: the parser validates `%` + two hex digits, then uses a percent-encode set that does not include `%`, so existing escapes appear to remain escapes rather than being decoded. (Inference from https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

**Uncertainty / Disagreement**

- There is direct evidence that this exact point was considered unclear enough to raise formally: whatwg/url issue `#565` asks whether parsing `http://example.com/%66%6f%6f` should yield `%66%6f%6f` or `foo`. The issue is labeled `clarification` and `editorial`, which suggests wording clarity rather than an intended behavioral change, but the issue itself is not normative. (https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/565)

**Lack Of Good Evidence**

- In the current parsing steps I reviewed, I found explicit rules for host IDNA conversion, default-port nulling, dot-segment removal, and fragment/path percent-encoding, but I did not find a separate explicit sentence that says “decode existing valid percent-encoded path bytes” or “uppercase their hex digits.” The strongest support for “preserve them” is the algorithmic inference above, not a single explicit prose rule. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/, https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/565)

So, under the current WHATWG URL Standard, the clear normalization steps are: lowercase the scheme, convert Unicode HTTPS hostnames to ASCII IDNA form, drop the default HTTPS port `443`, remove `.` and `..` path segments including `%2e` spellings, and percent-encode fragment/path characters according to their encode sets. For ordinary already-percent-encoded path bytes, the best reading of the current algorithm is preservation, not decoding or hex-case canonicalization, but that last point is inference rather than an explicit one-line rule.

# URL Standard: Key Parsing Details

## Host Parsing & IDNA

**Domain to ASCII (Section 3.3)**

The domain parser algorithm processes domains through Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing. Key steps include:

1. "Let strictResult be the result of running domain parser ToASCII with domain and true."
2. For non-ASCII strings: "Set result to the result of running domain parser ToASCII with domain and false."
3. "If result contains a forbidden domain code point, then return failure."

The domain parser ToASCII invokes Unicode's ToASCII algorithm with specific parameters: "CheckHyphens set to beStrict, CheckBidi set to true, CheckJoiners set to true, UseSTD3ASCIIRules set to beStrict."

**Percent-Decoding in Host Parsing (Section 3.5)**

Before domain processing: "Let domain be the result of running UTF-8 decode without BOM on the percent-decoding of input."

## Special Scheme Default Ports

**Port Handling (Section 4.4, Port State)**

When a port is parsed: "Set url's port to null, if port is url's scheme's default port; otherwise to port."

Default ports defined in Section 4.2:
- `http`: 80
- `https`: 443
- `ftp`: 21
- `ws`/`wss`: 80/443

## Path State & Dot Segments

**Dot Segment Processing (Section 4.4, Path State)**

The algorithm handles special segments:
- "A single-dot URL path segment is a URL path segment that is '.' or an ASCII case-insensitive match for '%2e'."
- "A double-dot URL path segment is a URL path segment that is '..' or an ASCII case-insensitive match for '.%2e', '%2e.', or '%2e%2e'."

Path shortening (Section 4.2): "Remove path's last item, if any."

## Fragment State & Percent-Encoding

**Fragment State (Section 4.4)**

The fragment state appends decoded code points to the fragment component.

**Fragment Percent-Encode Set (Section 1.3)**

"The fragment percent-encode set is a percent-encode set consisting of the C0 control percent-encode set and U+0020 SPACE, U+0022 ("), U+003C (<), U+003E (>), and U+0060 (`)."

## Percent-Encode Sets Hierarchy

# URL Standard Path and Encoding Details

## Path State
The path state steps include: "If [c](#c) is U+0000 NULL, [invalid-URL-unit](#invalid-url-unit) [validation error](#validation-error)." The state continues through various conditions handling slashes, dots, and other characters, ultimately appending code points to the URL's path.

## Shorten a URL's Path
Per the specification: "Assert: url does not have an [opaque path](#url-opaque-path). Let path be url's [path](#concept-url-path)." If conditions match a Windows drive letter on a file URL, the function returns without modification; otherwise it removes the final path item.

## Single-Dot and Double-Dot Segments
A single-dot segment is defined as "a [URL path segment](#url-path-segment) that is '`.`' or an [ASCII case-insensitive](#ascii-case-insensitive) match for '`%2e`'."

A double-dot segment represents "a [URL path segment](#url-path-segment) that is '`..`' or an [ASCII case-insensitive](#ascii-case-insensitive) match for '`.%2e`', '`%2e.`', or '`%2e%2e`'."

## Scheme Lowercasing
In scheme start state: "If [c](#c) is an [ASCII alpha](#ascii-alpha), append [c](#c), [lowercased](#ascii-lowercase), to buffer."

In scheme state: "append [c](#c), [lowercased](#ascii-lowercase), to buffer" for alphanumeric and symbol characters.

## Percent-Encoding Behavior
The specification notes: "Of the possible values for the percentEncodeSet argument only two end up encoding U+0025 (%) and thus give 'roundtripable data'" — indicating selective re-encoding based on context rather than blanket normalization of existing sequences.

# URL Standard Key Algorithms

## Host Parser Algorithm

The host parser accepts a scalar value string input with an optional boolean isOpaque (default false) and runs these steps:

1. **IPv6 handling**: "If input starts with U+005B (\[), then: If input does not end with U+005D (\]), [IPv6-unclosed](#ipv6-unclosed) [validation error](#validation-error), return failure."

2. **Percent-encoding check**: "If input contains a [percent-encoded byte](#percent-encoded-byte), [domain-percent-encoded](#domain-percent-encoded) [validation error](#validation-error)."

3. **Domain processing**: "Let domain be the result of running [UTF-8 decode without BOM](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#utf-8-decode-without-bom) on the [percent-decoding](#string-percent-decode) of input."

4. **ASCII domain**: "Let asciiDomain be the result of running [domain parser](#concept-domain-to-ascii) with domain and false."

5. **IPv4 check**: "If asciiDomain [ends in a number](#ends-in-a-number-checker): If domain is not an [ASCII string](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-string), [IPv4-non-ASCII-input](#ipv4-non-ascii-input) [validation error](#validation-error)."

# URL Parsing: Percent-Encoding Definitions

## Percent-Encoded Byte
"A percent-encoded byte is a string consisting of U+0025 (%) followed by two ASCII hex digits."

## Percent-Decode a Byte Sequence
The algorithm appends bytes to output, and "If byte is not 0x25 (%), then append byte to output." For percent sequences, it interprets the two following hex digits and appends the decoded byte value, skipping those two bytes in the process.

## UTF-8 Percent-Encode
"To UTF-8 percent-encode a scalar value string input using a percentEncodeSet, return the result of running percent-encode after encoding with UTF-8, input, and percentEncodeSet."

## Important Note on Non-Normalization
The specification emphasizes: "Of the possible values for the percentEncodeSet argument only two end up encoding U+0025 (%) and thus give 'roundtripable data': component percent-encode set and application/x-www-form-urlencoded percent-encode set. The other values...leave U+0025 (%) untouched..."

This indicates the parser treats existing percent-encoded sequences as literal text in certain contexts (like paths) rather than normalizing them.

# Path State and Fragment State from URL Standard

## Path State

The specification describes path state handling for double-dot and single-dot segments:

For double-dot segments: "If buffer is a double-dot URL path segment, then shorten url's path. If neither c is U+002F (/), nor url is special and c is U+005C (\\), append the empty string to url's path."

For single-dot segments: "If buffer is a single-dot URL path segment and if neither c is U+002F (/), nor url is special and c is U+005C (\\), append the empty string to url's path."

The path state processes these segments when encountering EOF, forward slashes, backslashes (for special URLs), or query/fragment markers.

# URL Standard: Fragment State and Parser Steps

## Fragment State

According to the specification, the fragment state operates as follows:

"If [c](#c) is the [EOF code point](#eof-code-point), U+003F (?), or U+0023 (#), then decrease pointer by 1, set url's [fragment](#concept-url-fragment) to buffer, and set state to [data state](#data-state)."

Otherwise, append the current code point to the fragment buffer.

## Basic URL Parser: Input Sanitization

The parser begins by handling problematic whitespace:

"If input contains any leading or trailing [C0 control or space](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#c0-control-or-space), [invalid-URL-unit](#invalid-url-unit) [validation error](#validation-error)."

Then it removes these characters entirely. Subsequently: "If input contains any [ASCII tab or newline](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#ascii-tab-or-newline), [invalid-URL-unit](#invalid-url-unit) [validation error](#validation-error)."

All such tab and newline characters are stripped from the input.

## URL Serializer: Port and Fragment

The serializer handles these components conditionally:

"If url's [port](#concept-url-port) is non-null and is not url's [scheme](#concept-url-scheme)'s [default port](#default-port), then append U+003A (:) followed by url's [port](#concept-url-port)."

For fragments: "If url's [fragment](#concept-url-fragment) is non-null, then append U+0023 (#) followed by url's [fragment](#concept-url-fragment)."

## Réponse courte

Le parseur d'URL de la [norme WHATWG URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) applique, pour une URL `https:` avec nom d'hôte Unicode, port par défaut, segments-points, fragment et octets percent-encodés dans le chemin, **six familles de normalisations** : nettoyage de l'entrée, minusculisation du schéma, conversion IDNA + minusculisation de l'hôte, mise à `null` du port par défaut, résolution des segments `.`/`..`, et percent-encodage sélectif du chemin et du fragment. Les séquences `%XX` déjà présentes ne sont **ni décodées ni normalisées en casse**.

---

## 1. Nettoyage préalable de l'entrée (« basic URL parser », étapes 1–2)

- Les *C0 control or space* en tête et en fin sont **retirés** (avec une `invalid-URL-unit` validation error). [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/review-drafts/2025-08/#fragment-state)
- **Tous** les ASCII tab/newline (U+0009, U+000A, U+000D) sont **supprimés**, où qu'ils soient. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/review-drafts/2025-08/#fragment-state)

C'est une normalisation destructrice : `ht\ntps://…` devient `https://…`.

## 2. Schéma → minuscules

Dans le *scheme start state* et le *scheme state*, le parseur fait « append c, **lowercased**, to buffer ». [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#path-state) Donc `HTTPS:` → `https:`.

## 3. Hôte Unicode → IDNA/Punycode + minuscules

Le *host parser* pour une URL spéciale :

1. Si l'entrée contient un *percent-encoded byte* → `domain-percent-encoded` validation error (non fatale). [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)
2. « Let domain be the result of running **UTF-8 decode without BOM** on the **percent-decoding** of input » — l'hôte est donc **percent-décodé avant** traitement. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)
3. « Let asciiDomain be the result of running **domain parser** with domain and **false** » (`beStrict = false`). [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)
4. Le *domain to ASCII* invoque **Unicode ToASCII (UTS #46)** avec `CheckHyphens = beStrict`, `CheckBidi = true`, `CheckJoiners = true`, `UseSTD3ASCIIRules = beStrict`, `Transitional_Processing = false`, `VerifyDnsLength = beStrict`, `IgnoreInvalidPunycode = false`. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) / [whatwg/url](https://github.com/whatwg/url/blob/main/url.bs)
5. Si le résultat contient un *forbidden domain code point* → `domain-invalid-code-point`, **échec** (erreur fatale). [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
6. Si `asciiDomain` *ends in a number*, il est traité par l'**IPv4 parser** (normalisation des formes octales/hexadécimales/entières en quatre nombres décimaux). [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)

Effets concrets : la normalisation Unicode (NFC, *mapping* de casse et de compatibilité) est celle de **UTS #46**, pas une opération propre à la norme URL ; `Transitional_Processing = false` signifie que `ß` et `ς` sont **préservés** (pas de conversion vers `ss`/`σ`). Comme optimisation web-compatible, si `beStrict` est faux et que le domaine est déjà une chaîne ASCII, l'algorithme renvoie le domaine **en minuscules** quel que soit le résultat de ToASCII. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) Donc `ExAmPlE.COM` → `example.com`, et `bücher.example` → `xn--bcher-kva.example`.

## 4. Port par défaut → `null`

Table des schémas spéciaux : `ftp` 21, `file` null, `http` 80, **`https` 443**, `ws` 80, `wss` 443. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)

Dans le *port state* : « Set url's port to **null**, if port is url's scheme's default port; otherwise to port. » [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-host-parser)

Le *URL serializer* n'émet le `:port` que si le port est non-null ; la suppression de `:443` est donc **acquise dès le parsing**, pas à la sérialisation. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/review-drafts/2025-08/) Autre effet : les zéros de tête sont absorbés (le port est stocké comme entier).

## 5. Segments-points (`.` / `..`)

Définitions (notez qu'elles couvrent les formes **percent-encodées**) :

- *single-dot URL path segment* = « `.` » ou une correspondance **ASCII case-insensitive** de « `%2e` ». [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#path-state)
- *double-dot URL path segment* = « `..` » ou une correspondance ASCII case-insensitive de « `.%2e` », « `%2e.` » ou « `%2e%2e` ». [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#path-state)

Traitement dans le *path state* :

> « If buffer is a double-dot URL path segment, then **shorten url's path**. If neither c is U+002F (/), nor url is special and c is U+005C (\\), **append the empty string** to url's path. »
> « If buffer is a single-dot URL path segment and if neither c is U+002F (/), nor url is special and c is U+005C (\\), append the empty string to url's path. » [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/review-drafts/2025-08/#path-state)

*Shorten a URL's path* = « Remove path's last item, if any », avec l'exception des lettres de lecteur Windows pour `file:`. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#path-state) L'ajout de la chaîne vide garantit que `/usr/..` donne `/` et non un chemin vide. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

Deux points souvent mal compris, et **factuellement établis** par les définitions ci-dessus :
- `%2E` (en n'importe quelle casse) **est** traité comme un point pour la détection des segments-points ;
- pour une URL spéciale, `\` est traité comme `/` (donc `..\` fonctionne aussi comme remontée).

À noter aussi : pour les URLs spéciales, un `..` en tête ne peut pas remonter au-dessus de la racine, puisque `shorten` retire simplement le dernier élément d'un chemin déjà vide (aucun effet). *— inférence directe de la définition, non citée telle quelle.*

## 6. Percent-encodage du chemin et du fragment

Ensembles pertinents : [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

- *C0 control percent-encode set* = les C0 controls **et tous les code points > U+007E** ;
- *path percent-encode set* = *query percent-encode set* + `?` `^` `` ` `` `{` `}` ;
- *fragment percent-encode set* = *C0 control set* + espace, `"`, `<`, `>`, `` ` ``.

Le chemin est encodé via *UTF-8 percent-encode* avec le *path percent-encode set*, le fragment via le *fragment percent-encode set*. [github.com/whatwg/url](https://github.com/whatwg/url/commit/7a3c69f8a1583b33e730c3fea85141a618e7c697) Conséquence : tout caractère non-ASCII dans le chemin ou le fragment est **encodé en UTF-8 puis percent-encodé** (car > U+007E).

**Les octets déjà percent-encodés sont laissés tels quels.** La norme note que « of the possible values for the percentEncodeSet argument only two end up encoding U+0025 (%) […] : component percent-encode set and application/x-www-form-urlencoded percent-encode set. The other values […] leave U+0025 (%) untouched ». [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#percent-encoded-bytes) Ni le *path percent-encode set* ni le *fragment percent-encode set* n'incluent `%` : donc `%41` reste `%41` (pas de décodage vers `A`), et `%2f` reste `%2f` (pas de minusculisation/majusculisation des chiffres hexadécimaux).

**Il n'y a donc pas** de normalisation « RFC 3986 §6.2.2.1/2.2 » (majuscules des hex-digits, décodage des *unreserved characters*) dans la norme WHATWG. *— Il s'agit d'une inférence par absence : je n'ai trouvé aucune étape prescrivant cette normalisation, et la note ci-dessus la contredit implicitement ; la norme ne l'énonce pas explicitement comme un « non-fait ».*

Enfin, le fragment est **conservé** par le parseur ; seule la variante *URL serializer* avec `exclude fragment` le retire. [url.spec.whatwg.org](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/review-drafts/2025-08/#fragment-state)
